column1: # topic: Chapter 4: Colonization and Conflict in the North

column2: Jacques Cartier led the first official French expedition to what the French called Canada, sailing through the Gulf of St. Lawrence.
Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec far up the St. Lawrence to trade furs with less European competition and bound New France to the Montagnais, Algonquins and Hurons.
The Hurons were a confederacy of farmers 20,000 strong near Georgian Bay, France's chief fur-trade allies until smallpox and Iroquois attacks destroyed them.
The Iroquois League was a confederacy of five nations, the Mohawks, Oneidas, Onondagas, Cayugas and Senecas, that used Dutch trade guns to wage the Beaver Wars.
The Mohawks were the Iroquois nation that took over the Dutch fur trade at Fort Orange, giving the Iroquois the tools and guns to attack their northern enemies.
The Jesuits, or Society of Jesus, were Catholic missionaries fired by the Counter-Reformation whom French authorities sent to live among Indian allies and convert them.
The Huguenots were French Protestants, France's most obvious emigrants, whom French monarchs barred from Canada because they insisted New France stay Catholic.

column1: René Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle
column2: La Salle was the first European to travel down the Mississippi to the Gulf of Mexico, extending French claims and alliances into the Mississippi valley.

The Puritans were radical English Protestant reformers who followed Calvin and wanted to purify the Church of England, split into Presbyterians, whose congregations answered to higher bodies of ministers and laypersons, and Congregationalists.
Congregationalists were Puritans whose congregations ran their own affairs independently, and most of them still believed the Church of England could be reformed from within.
Separatists were devout Congregationalists who concluded the Church of England was too corrupt to reform, so they left it and worshiped secretly in small congregations.
The Pilgrims were the Separatists who sailed on the Mayflower and founded Plymouth Colony after first trying exile in Holland.
Massasoit was the Wampanoag chief who, weakened by epidemic and eager for trade goods and help against native enemies, agreed to help the starving Plymouth colonists.
Squanto was a Wampanoag kidnapped by English sailors and taught English in Europe, who returned in time to serve as the go-between for the Pilgrims and Massasoit.
John Winthrop was the lawyer and first governor of Massachusetts Bay who founded Boston and wanted a godly "city on a hill" whose settlers would be "knit together" as one.
Roger Williams was a Salem minister who called for separation from the Church of England and of church and state, denied the king's right to Indian land, and founded Providence.
Anne Hutchinson was a Boston midwife whose sermon discussions and controversial doctrine led ministers to accuse her of heresy and the colony to expel her.
Salem was the Massachusetts town where accusations by a group of afflicted adolescent girls in Salem Village led to the largest witchcraft trials and twenty executions in New England.
Metacom, Massasoit's son whom the English called King Philip, led southern New England's Indians in a war against the colonists that ended in his death and his people's ruin.
As Duke of York, James took New Netherland and renamed it New York, and as King James II he created the Dominion of New England and abolished colonial assemblies until Parliament overthrew him.
William Penn, son of an admiral, was a Quaker leader who founded Pennsylvania as a refuge for Quakers with freedom of worship and fair dealing with the Indians.
The Quakers, formally the Society of Friends, dressed plainly, refused oaths, war and bows to superiors, let women preach, and found refuge in Pennsylvania and New Jersey.
Philadelphia, on a superb harbor where the Delaware and Schuylkill Rivers meet, was Pennsylvania's trade center and became the commercial and cultural center of England's North American empire.
William of Orange and Mary, James II's Protestant daughter, took the throne in the Glorious Revolution, agreed to rule with Parliament, and restored colonial assemblies.
